records.source: Οὕτως ἡμᾶς λογιζέσθω ἄνθρωπος ὡς ὑπηρέτας Χριστοῦ καὶ οἰκονόμους μυστηρίων θεοῦ.
records.gloss: So us let regard a man as assistants of Christ and stewards of mysteries of God.
pieces: So {{gender:people|men}} should think of us in this way: as assistants of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} and as household managers put in charge of the mysteries of God.

L.1: So let a {{gender:person|man}} regard us: as assistants of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} and stewards of [the] mysteries of God.

R.1: So this is how everyone should think of us. We are helpers who work for {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. God has put us in charge of the secrets {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has now made known.

decisions.choice: so ... as: "so" points forward to the description that follows
decisions.reason: Οὕτως is picked up by ὡς: "in this way ... as". Paul has just said that he and Apollos belong to the church (3:22); now he says how the church should rate its teachers.

decisions.choice: assistants: helpers under the orders of a superior
decisions.reason: ὑπηρέτας was used of attendants and subordinates who carried out another's orders: the synagogue attendant (Luke 4:20), officers of a court (Matthew 5:25). The word stresses that Paul and Apollos act under Christ's direction, not on their own authority.

decisions.choice: household managers: people, often slaves, who ran a household's affairs for its owner and answered to him
alternatives: stewards in a general modern sense
decisions.reason: An οἰκονόμους managed a master's property, goods and staff (Luke 12:42; 16:1-8). He had real authority over the household but was accountable to the owner. Verse 2 builds on this: what matters in such a manager is that he can be trusted.

decisions.choice: mysteries of God: God's purposes, once hidden and now made known in the gospel
alternatives: secret rites, as in the mystery cults
decisions.reason: Paul has spoken of "the mystery of God" (2:1) and "God's wisdom in a mystery, which was hidden" (2:7): God's plan of salvation through the crucified Christ, now revealed by the Spirit. A mystery in this sense is not a puzzle but a secret disclosed.

decisions.choice: assistants (L, B); helpers who work for (R)
decisions.reason: "Servants" is too general and "ministers" suggests a church office. "Assistants" keeps the idea of someone carrying out a superior's orders.

decisions.choice: household managers put in charge of the mysteries (B); put us in charge of the secrets he has now made known (R)
decisions.reason: "Steward" is little used today; Balanced names the role. Readable says what a mystery is in Paul's sense (meaning note m4), since "mystery" now suggests a puzzle or a crime story.

decisions.choice: {{gender:person|man}} (L); {{gender:people|men}} (B)
decisions.reason: ἄνθρωπος is general: anyone at all. Readable says "everyone", which needs no setting.

records.heading: Managers answerable to the Lord

records.source: ὧδε λοιπὸν ζητεῖται ἐν τοῖς οἰκονόμοις ἵνα πιστός τις εὑρεθῇ.
records.gloss: Here moreover it is sought in the stewards that faithful someone be found.
pieces: Now what is looked for in household managers is this: that each one proves trustworthy.

L.2: Here, moreover, it is sought in stewards that one be found faithful.

R.2: And the most important thing about people put in charge of a household is that they can be trusted.

decisions.choice: in this connection, moreover: a further point drawn from the picture of the manager
alternatives: "here on earth", in contrast to the Lord's judgment in verse 4
decisions.reason: ὧδε can mean "here" or "in this case", and λοιπὸν can mean "furthermore" or "as for the rest". Together they introduce what follows from calling the apostles managers: the one quality that counts in such a person.

decisions.choice: trustworthy, reliable in the task given
decisions.reason: πιστός can mean "believing" or "faithful". Said of a manager, it means one who handles the master's affairs loyally and well. The verb εὑρεθῇ ("be found") suggests that the manager's record is examined, which leads into verses 3-5.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "it is sought" (passive)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts have the second-person form, "you seek", which was pronounced almost the same in later Greek. The SBLGNT follows the passive, which fits the general statement. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: proves trustworthy (B); can be trusted (R)
decisions.reason: "Faithful" can suggest religious belief or marital loyalty; the point is reliability in a task. Literal keeps "found faithful".

records.source: ἐμοὶ δὲ εἰς ἐλάχιστόν ἐστιν, ἵνα ὑφ’ ὑμῶν ἀνακριθῶ ἢ ὑπὸ ἀνθρωπίνης ἡμέρας· ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ ἐμαυτὸν ἀνακρίνω·
records.gloss: To me but for a very small thing it is that by you I be examined or by human day; but not even myself do I examine;
pieces: For my part, it counts for very little if you put me on trial, or if any human court does. I do not even put myself on trial.

L.3: But to me it is a very small thing that I should be examined by you or by [a] human day; indeed, I do not even examine myself.

R.3: It does not matter much to me if you put me on trial, or if any human court does. I do not even sit as my own judge.

decisions.choice: examine: question and assess, as in a court hearing
alternatives: judge in the sense of condemn
decisions.reason: ἀνακριθῶ was used for the questioning of a person at a hearing before a verdict (Acts 4:9; 12:19). Paul has used the same verb in 2:14-15 of the spiritual person who examines all things. Some in Corinth were weighing up their teachers against one another (1:12; 3:4).

decisions.choice: a human day: a human court, or a day of hearing set by people
decisions.reason: "Day" was used of the day set for a trial, hence a court. "Human day" contrasts with "the day" of 3:13, the day of the Lord, when the true worth of each one's work will be shown.

decisions.choice: indeed, not even: Paul goes further than declining their verdict
alternatives: but I do not examine myself (a contrast)
decisions.reason: οὐδὲ adds a stronger point: Paul is not even his own judge. The reason follows in verse 4.

decisions.choice: put me on trial; any human court
decisions.reason: "Put on trial" keeps the courtroom setting of the verb; "human court" says what "human day" means. Literal keeps "human day" and the note explains it.

records.source: οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐν τούτῳ δεδικαίωμαι, ὁ δὲ ἀνακρίνων με κύριός ἐστιν.
records.gloss: Nothing for against myself I am aware of, but not by this I have been justified; the [one] but examining me Lord is.
pieces: I know of nothing I have done wrong, yet that is not what acquits me. The one who examines my case is the Lord.

L.4: For I am aware of nothing against myself, but I have not been justified by this; rather, the one who examines me is [the] Lord.

R.4: I do not know of anything wrong that I have done. But that does not mean I am in the right. The Lord is the one who judges me.

decisions.choice: I am not conscious of any fault
decisions.reason: ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα means to share knowledge with oneself, the root of the word for conscience. Paul says his conscience does not accuse him in his work as Christ's manager. He does not claim to be without sin; he says that even a clear conscience settles nothing.

decisions.choice: acquitted: declared in the right by a judge
alternatives: justified, in the sense of a sinner being put right with God
decisions.reason: δεδικαίωμαι is a courtroom word: to declare someone in the right. Here the question is the verdict on Paul's service, so the sense is "acquitted". The same verb carries Paul's teaching that God puts sinners right with himself (Romans 3:24-28), but that is not the subject here, though the thought is related: only the Lord's verdict counts.

decisions.choice: the Lord: Christ, who will come as judge
decisions.reason: Verse 5 speaks of "the Lord" coming and of praise "from God", which distinguishes the two. Paul regularly calls Jesus "Lord" (1:2-3, 7-8), and he speaks of standing before Christ's judgment seat (2 Corinthians 5:10).

decisions.choice: acquits
decisions.reason: "Justify" in current English means to give reasons for something; "acquit" keeps the courtroom sense. Literal keeps "justified" so the reader can see the word Paul uses elsewhere.

records.source: ὥστε μὴ πρὸ καιροῦ τι κρίνετε, ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ ὁ κύριος, ὃς καὶ φωτίσει τὰ κρυπτὰ τοῦ σκότους καὶ φανερώσει τὰς βουλὰς τῶν καρδιῶν, καὶ τότε ὁ ἔπαινος γενήσεται ἑκάστῳ ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: So that not before time anything judge, until comes the Lord, who also will bring to light the hidden things of the darkness and will make manifest the purposes of the hearts, and then the praise will come to each from the God.
pieces: So do not pass sentence on anything ahead of time, before the Lord comes. He will shine light on what darkness now hides and bring the purposes of all hearts out into the open. Then each one will have from God whatever praise is due.

L.5: So do not judge anything before [the] time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of the darkness and make known the purposes of the hearts; and then the praise will come to each one from God.

R.5: So do not judge anyone before the right time. Wait until the Lord comes back. He will bring out into the light the things that are hidden in the dark. He will show what people really wanted in their hearts. Then God will praise each one as that person deserves.

decisions.choice: stop passing verdicts: a ban on judging before the time
alternatives: never form any opinion of others
decisions.reason: κρίνετε is a present command with a negative, which can mean "stop doing" what is already going on. The Corinthians were already ranking their teachers. Paul forbids a final verdict now, not all discernment (compare 5:12).

decisions.choice: the time: the appointed time of the Lord's coming
decisions.reason: πρὸ καιροῦ is explained by the next clause: the time is when the Lord comes, the "day" of 1:8 and 3:13.

decisions.choice: what is now hidden, and the purposes of the heart
alternatives: only evil deeds done in secret
decisions.reason: "The hidden things of darkness" are whatever is now out of sight, good or bad, not only sins. The "heart" is where a person thinks and decides, so βουλὰς are the motives behind actions, which no human judge can see.

decisions.choice: the praise due to each: God will give the commendation each one deserves
decisions.reason: The article with ἔπαινος points to the praise belonging to each person. Paul speaks of praise because he is warning against human verdicts, but 3:13-15 shows that the Lord's judgment can also bring loss.

decisions.choice: comes back
decisions.reason: The Lord's coming is his return (1:7-8); Readable says so.

records.source: Ταῦτα δέ, ἀδελφοί, μετεσχημάτισα εἰς ἐμαυτὸν καὶ Ἀπολλῶν δι’ ὑμᾶς, ἵνα ἐν ἡμῖν μάθητε τό· Μὴ ὑπὲρ ἃ γέγραπται, ἵνα μὴ εἷς ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἑνὸς φυσιοῦσθε κατὰ τοῦ ἑτέρου.
records.gloss: These things now, brothers, I transferred to myself and Apollos because of you, so that in us you may learn the "Not beyond what is written," so that not one on behalf of the one you be puffed up against the other.
pieces: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I have used myself and Apollos as the picture for all this, for your sake. From us you can learn what is meant by "Nothing beyond what is written," and then none of you will be puffed up in favor of one person and against another.

L.6: Now these things, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, I have applied to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you may learn the [saying], "Not beyond what is written," so that you are not puffed up, one on behalf of the one against the other.

R.6: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I have been talking about Apollos and me to make all this clear to you. I want you to learn from us what this saying means: "Keep within what is written." Then you will not be proud of one leader and look down on another.

decisions.choice: applied as an illustration: Paul has used himself and Apollos as the example, so that the lesson reaches every teacher and every faction
alternatives: simply "I have applied these things to myself"
I have disguised these things: a veiled reference to other leaders whom Paul does not name
decisions.reason: μετεσχημάτισα means to change the form of something. Paul has spoken of himself and Apollos as planter and waterer, builders and managers (3:5-4:5). He chose the two of them, who were on good terms, as a figure for a lesson that applies to the whole church's habit of rallying behind teachers. Exactly how much the verb implies is debated.

decisions.choice: a saying, most likely about keeping within Scripture
alternatives: a rule about a written agreement
a copyist's note that later entered the text
decisions.reason: The article τό marks the words that follow as a quotation, and they have no verb. In this letter "it is written" introduces Scripture (1:19, 31; 3:19-20), and the passages Paul has quoted all warn against human pride and boasting (1:31, from Jeremiah 9:24). So the saying most likely means: do not go beyond what Scripture says. The words are so brief that no explanation is certain.

decisions.choice: so that none of you is puffed up for one teacher against another
alternatives: so that no teacher is puffed up against another
decisions.reason: "One for the one against the other" describes believers taking sides: each praising one leader and running down another, as 1:12 and 3:4 describe. φυσιοῦσθε has an indicative ending after ἵνα, an irregular form, but the sense is purpose.

decisions.choice: puffed up: inflated with self-importance
decisions.reason: φυσιοῦσθε pictures something blown up with air. Paul uses the verb six times in this letter for the arrogance he sees in Corinth (4:18-19; 5:2; 8:1; 13:4), and nowhere else except Colossians 2:18.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} ({{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}} at the start of a sentence)
decisions.reason: Paul addresses the whole church, women and men (1:11 names Chloe's people).

decisions.choice: Keep within what is written
alternatives: Do not go beyond what is written
decisions.reason: Readable turns the verbless saying into a plain instruction, keeping its open wording rather than adding "Scripture", since the meaning is uncertain (m2).

records.heading: Nothing you were not given

records.source: τίς γάρ σε διακρίνει;
records.gloss: Who for you distinguishes?
pieces: Who, after all, sets you above anyone else?

R.7: Who decided that you are better than anyone else?

decisions.choice: sets apart as superior
decisions.reason: διακρίνει means to separate or distinguish. Here it means to treat someone as better than others. The expected answer is "no one": nothing makes one believer superior to another.

decisions.choice: you, singular: Paul addresses each reader directly
decisions.reason: σε is singular. In the next three questions Paul speaks to the individual who is puffed up, a lively style of argument common in moral teaching of the time.

decisions.choice: above anyone else (B); better than anyone else (R)
decisions.reason: The verb implies being ranked above others; Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: τί δὲ ἔχεις ὃ οὐκ ἔλαβες;
records.gloss: What and do you have which not you received?
pieces: What do you have that was not given to you?

L.7: And what do you have that you did not receive?

R.7: Is there anything you have that was not given to you?

decisions.choice: everything a believer has is a gift from God
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer "nothing". Paul has already said that God enriched the Corinthians with every gift (1:4-7) and that Christ became their wisdom (1:30). Gifts give no ground for pride.

decisions.choice: was not given to you
decisions.reason: The passive brings out that what they have came from someone else; the next question turns on this.

records.source: εἰ δὲ καὶ ἔλαβες, τί καυχᾶσαι ὡς μὴ λαβών;
records.gloss: If and also you received, why do you boast as not having received?
pieces: And if it was given to you, why do you take pride in it as though it were not a gift?

L.7: And if you did receive [it], why do you boast as if you had not received [it]?

R.7: And if it was a gift, why do you brag as if you had earned it yourself?

decisions.choice: boast: take pride in something as one's own
decisions.reason: καυχᾶσαι means to boast or pride oneself. The letter has already said that no one may boast before God, except in the Lord (1:29-31; 3:21).

decisions.choice: as if it were not received: as if it were one's own achievement
decisions.reason: λαβών describes the attitude of someone acting as though a gift were their own doing.

decisions.choice: as if you had earned it yourself
alternatives: as if you had not received it
decisions.reason: Readable states what boasting about a gift implies.

decisions.choice: take pride in it (B); brag (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "boast" so the word can be traced through both letters. Balanced says "take pride" except where Paul's argument turns on the word itself (1:29-31; 2 Corinthians 10-12), and Readable uses "brag" for pride that takes credit for a gift (m1, m2).

records.source: Ἤδη κεκορεσμένοι ἐστέ, ἤδη ἐπλουτήσατε, χωρὶς ἡμῶν ἐβασιλεύσατε· καὶ ὄφελόν γε ἐβασιλεύσατε, ἵνα καὶ ἡμεῖς ὑμῖν συμβασιλεύσωμεν.
records.gloss: Already filled you are, already you became rich, without us you reigned; and I wish indeed you reigned, so that also we with you might reign.
pieces: So you are already full! You are already rich! Without us you have begun to rule as kings! If only you really did rule, so that we too could rule alongside you!

L.8: Already you are filled! Already you have become rich! Without us you have begun to reign! And I wish indeed that you did reign, so that we also might reign with you.

R.8: You think you already have everything you need! You think you are already rich! You act as if you were already kings, and you did not need us! I really wish you were kings, because then we would be kings with you.

decisions.choice: irony: Paul repeats what the Corinthians think of themselves in order to expose it
alternatives: the same words read as questions: "Are you already full?"
a plain statement of their blessings
decisions.reason: Verses 9-13 set the apostles' real condition beside these claims, which shows the words are ironic. The SBLGNT punctuates them as statements; read as questions they make the same point.

decisions.choice: they act as if the age to come had fully arrived
decisions.reason: Believers will reign with Christ in the age to come (6:2-3; 2 Timothy 2:12). The repeated Ἤδη suggests the Corinthians speak as though they already have that fullness, wealth and rule, "without us", that is, without needing the apostles who brought them the gospel.

decisions.choice: you have begun to reign, you have come to rule
decisions.reason: ἐβασιλεύσατε is an aorist that here marks entry into a state: they have become kings.

decisions.choice: a wish that is not true: if only you did reign
decisions.reason: ὄφελόν introduces a wish that cannot be or has not been fulfilled. If the kingdom had really come, the apostles would share in it too; their suffering shows that it has not.

decisions.choice: You think ...
decisions.reason: Readable makes the irony plain, since young readers may take the words at face value.

records.source: δοκῶ γάρ, ὁ θεὸς ἡμᾶς τοὺς ἀποστόλους ἐσχάτους ἀπέδειξεν ὡς ἐπιθανατίους, ὅτι θέατρον ἐγενήθημεν τῷ κόσμῳ καὶ ἀγγέλοις καὶ ἀνθρώποις.
records.gloss: I think for, the God us the apostles last displayed as condemned to death, because spectacle we became to the world, both to angels and to men.
pieces: As I see it, God has brought us apostles out last of all, like condemned prisoners led in to die. We have become a show for the world to watch, angels and {{gender:human beings|men}} alike.

L.9: For I think, God has displayed us, the apostles, last, as [those] condemned to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, both to angels and to {{gender:human beings|men}}.

R.9: I think God has made us apostles the lowest of all. We are like prisoners who are brought out at the end of the show to be killed while everyone watches. The whole world is staring at us, both angels and {{gender:people|men}}.

decisions.choice: put on show last, like people condemned to die in public
alternatives: the captives led at the end of a Roman triumph, to be executed afterward
decisions.reason: ἀπέδειξεν means to put on display, and ἐπιθανατίους describes people sentenced to death. In the Roman world condemned criminals were brought into the arena at the end of the shows to die before the crowd, and captives were paraded in a general's triumph before their execution (compare 2 Corinthians 2:14). Either picture fits; both describe public humiliation ending in death.

decisions.choice: a spectacle: something people gather to stare at
decisions.reason: θέατρον was the theater and also what was shown there. The apostles have become the show.

decisions.choice: the world, that is, angels as well as humans
decisions.reason: The repeated "and ... and" spells out who "the world" is here: the whole created order, heavenly and earthly, watches what happens to the apostles.

decisions.choice: brought out at the end of the show to be killed
decisions.reason: Readable describes the arena picture, one of the two possible backgrounds (m1).

decisions.choice: {{gender:human beings|men}} (L, B); {{gender:people|men}} (R)
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώποις means human beings in general, set beside the angels.

records.source: ἡμεῖς μωροὶ διὰ Χριστόν, ὑμεῖς δὲ φρόνιμοι ἐν Χριστῷ· ἡμεῖς ἀσθενεῖς, ὑμεῖς δὲ ἰσχυροί· ὑμεῖς ἔνδοξοι, ἡμεῖς δὲ ἄτιμοι.
records.gloss: We fools because of Christ, you but wise in Christ; we weak, you but strong; you honored, we but without honor.
pieces: We are fools because of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, but you are so wise in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}! We are weak, but you are strong! You are held in honor, but we are despised.

L.10: We [are] fools because of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, but you [are] wise in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}; we [are] weak, but you [are] strong; you [are] honored, but we [are] without honor.

R.10: People think we are fools because we follow {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. But you think you are so wise because you belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}! We are weak, but you are strong! People respect you, but they look down on us.

decisions.choice: ironic contrasts: the Corinthians' view of themselves set against the apostles' lot
decisions.reason: This continues the irony of verse 8. In 1:18-25 Paul has shown that God chose what the world counts foolish and weak; the Corinthians want to be thought wise and strong, the very things he has said God sets aside.

decisions.choice: fools ... wise: as people judge
decisions.reason: μωροὶ and φρόνιμοι take up the language of 1:18-3:20. The apostles look foolish because they preach Christ crucified; the Corinthians consider themselves sensible people.

decisions.choice: honored ... dishonored: social standing
decisions.reason: ἔνδοξοι and ἄτιμοι are words of public reputation and rank. Notice that the last pair reverses the order, ending on the apostles' disgrace.

decisions.choice: People think we are fools because we follow; you think you are so wise because you belong to
alternatives: We are fools because of; you are wise in
decisions.reason: Readable makes the irony explicit, as in verse 8.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

records.source: ἄχρι τῆς ἄρτι ὥρας καὶ πεινῶμεν καὶ διψῶμεν καὶ γυμνιτεύομεν καὶ κολαφιζόμεθα καὶ ἀστατοῦμεν καὶ κοπιῶμεν ἐργαζόμενοι ταῖς ἰδίαις χερσίν· λοιδορούμενοι εὐλογοῦμεν, διωκόμενοι ἀνεχόμεθα, δυσφημούμενοι παρακαλοῦμεν· ὡς περικαθάρματα τοῦ κόσμου ἐγενήθημεν, πάντων περίψημα ἕως ἄρτι.
records.gloss: Until the present hour both we hunger and we thirst and we are poorly clothed and we are struck and we are homeless \v 12 and we labor working with the own hands; being reviled we bless, being persecuted we endure, \v 13 being slandered we appeal; as scum of the world we became, of all things scrapings until now.
pieces: Even now, at this very hour, we are hungry and thirsty, dressed in rags, beaten, with no place to call home.
We toil, working with our own hands. Insulted, we bless; persecuted, we hold out;
slandered, we reply with kind words. Right up to now we are treated like the dirt the world sweeps away, the scrapings everyone throws out.

L.11: Up to the present hour we both hunger and thirst, and we are poorly clothed and are beaten and are homeless,
L.12: and we labor, working with [our] own hands. Being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we endure;
L.13: being slandered, we speak kindly. We have become like [the] scum of the world, [the] scrapings of all [things], until now.

R.11: Even now we are hungry and thirsty. Our clothes are worn out. People beat us. We have no home.
R.12: We work hard with our own hands to earn a living. When people insult us, we ask God to be good to them. When people attack us, we put up with it.
R.13: When people say evil things about us, we answer them kindly. Even now, people treat us like garbage, like the dirt that everyone in the world throws away.

decisions.choice: poorly clothed, roughly treated, without a settled home
decisions.reason: γυμνιτεύομεν means to be scantily dressed, not naked. κολαφιζόμεθα is to be struck with the fist, or treated roughly. ἀστατοῦμεν is to be unsettled, moving from place to place with no home of one's own. Paul lists the same hardships in 2 Corinthians 11:23-27.

decisions.choice: manual labor to support themselves
decisions.reason: Paul worked at a trade, making tents, while he was in Corinth (Acts 18:3), so as not to be a burden (9:12-18; 1 Thessalonians 2:9). People of standing in Greek cities often looked down on manual work; the Corinthians who prized status may have thought it beneath an apostle.

decisions.choice: blessing those who curse: the way Jesus taught
decisions.reason: Answering insult with blessing and persecution with endurance follows Jesus' teaching (Luke 6:27-28; Matthew 5:44), which Paul also gives in Romans 12:14. To εὐλογοῦμεν is to speak well of someone and ask God's good for them.

decisions.choice: speak kindly, appeal in a friendly way
decisions.reason: παρακαλοῦμεν has many senses: urge, appeal, comfort. Set against slander, it means answering with gentle words and trying to win people over rather than hitting back.

decisions.choice: scum, scrapings: the dirt removed in cleaning, and so the most worthless of people
alternatives: a scapegoat: a person thrown out or killed to cleanse a city
decisions.reason: περικαθάρματα is what is swept up when something is cleaned, and περίψημα what is scraped or rubbed off. Both words were also used in insults for worthless people. The first was used, too, of people who were driven out or put to death as an offering to rid a city of disaster, and some hear that sense here; the context of contempt does not require it.

decisions.choice: to earn a living
decisions.reason: Readable says why Paul worked with his hands, which the first readers knew (m2).

decisions.choice: we ask God to be good to them
decisions.reason: "Bless" is church language for many readers; Readable says what it means here (m3).

records.source: Οὐκ ἐντρέπων ὑμᾶς γράφω ταῦτα, ἀλλ’ ὡς τέκνα μου ἀγαπητὰ νουθετῶν·
records.gloss: Not shaming you I write these things, but as children of me beloved admonishing;
pieces: I do not write this to shame you. You are my dear children, and I am giving you a father's warning.

L.14: I do not write these things shaming you, but admonishing [you] as my beloved children.

R.14: I am not writing these things to make you feel ashamed. You are my children, and I love you. I want to warn you and help you do what is right.

decisions.choice: put to shame, humiliate
decisions.reason: ἐντρέπων means to make someone ashamed. The irony of verses 8-13 was sharp, so Paul says plainly what it was for.

decisions.choice: admonish: warn and correct, as a parent does
decisions.reason: νουθετῶν means to put sense into someone: to warn and correct with instruction. It is what a father does for his children (Ephesians 6:4 uses the related noun), which leads into verse 15.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "admonishing" (participle)
decisions.reason: Some important manuscripts have the finite verb, "I admonish you", instead of the participle. The meaning is the same. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a father's warning
decisions.reason: Verse 15 says Paul is their father; Balanced brings that into the picture of admonishing "as my dear children".

decisions.choice: help you do what is right
decisions.reason: Readable explains that admonishing aims at correction.

records.heading: A father's warning

records.source: ἐὰν γὰρ μυρίους παιδαγωγοὺς ἔχητε ἐν Χριστῷ, ἀλλ’ οὐ πολλοὺς πατέρας, ἐν γὰρ Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ διὰ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου ἐγὼ ὑμᾶς ἐγέννησα.
records.gloss: If for ten thousand guardians you have in Christ, yet not many fathers; in for Christ Jesus through the gospel I you fathered.
pieces: Though you may have countless guides to bring you up in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, you do not have many fathers. For it was I who fathered you in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus, through the gospel.

L.15: For if you have 10,000 guardians in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, yet [you have] not many fathers; for in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus through the gospel I fathered you.

R.15: You may have thousands of people to guide you in your life with {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. But you do not have many fathers. I became your father when I brought you the good news and you came to belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

decisions.choice: guardians: household slaves who looked after a boy and saw to his conduct
decisions.reason: A παιδαγωγοὺς was usually a slave who took a boy to school, watched over his behavior and disciplined him until he came of age (Galatians 3:24-25). He was not the father, and usually not the teacher either. Paul means the many who have instructed the Corinthians since he left; none of them is their father.

decisions.choice: ten thousand: countless
decisions.reason: μυρίους is the largest Greek number word and was commonly used for a number too great to count. Paul exaggerates on purpose.

decisions.choice: fathered: brought them to new life
decisions.reason: ἐγέννησα is used of a father begetting a child. Paul brought the church into being by preaching the gospel in Corinth (Acts 18:1-11); he has called himself the one who planted (3:6). It is a picture of a lasting family bond, not of authority alone.

decisions.choice: 10,000 guardians (L); countless guides to bring you up (B); thousands of people to guide you (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the number, written in figures as the style requires. Balanced and Readable give its sense, and "guide" avoids "tutor", which now means a private teacher.

decisions.choice: when I brought you the good news and you came to belong to
alternatives: in Christ Jesus through the gospel I fathered you
decisions.reason: Readable turns the picture of fathering into the events it describes.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

records.source: παρακαλῶ οὖν ὑμᾶς, μιμηταί μου γίνεσθε.
records.gloss: I urge therefore you, imitators of me become.
pieces: So I urge you: take me as your example.

L.16: I urge you therefore, become imitators of me.

R.16: So I am asking you to live the way I live.

decisions.choice: copy me, as children copy their father
decisions.reason: Coming after verse 15, μιμηταί draws on the idea that children learn by copying their father, and pupils their teacher. Paul's own model is Christ (11:1), and what he means is the way of life described in verses 9-13, not his personality.

decisions.choice: urge, appeal to
decisions.reason: παρακαλῶ is the verb of 1:10, where Paul appeals to the church to be united.

decisions.choice: take me as your example (B); live the way I live (R)
decisions.reason: "Imitate" can suggest mimicry; the sense is following a pattern of life.

records.source: διὰ τοῦτο ἔπεμψα ὑμῖν Τιμόθεον, ὅς ἐστίν μου τέκνον ἀγαπητὸν καὶ πιστὸν ἐν κυρίῳ, ὃς ὑμᾶς ἀναμνήσει τὰς ὁδούς μου τὰς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, καθὼς πανταχοῦ ἐν πάσῃ ἐκκλησίᾳ διδάσκω.
records.gloss: Because of this I sent to you Timothy, who is of me child beloved and faithful in Lord, who you will remind of the ways of me the in Christ Jesus, just as everywhere in every church I teach.
pieces: That is the reason I have sent Timothy to you. He is my dear child in the Lord, and he can be trusted. He will bring back to your minds the way I live in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus, the same way I teach in every church everywhere.

L.17: For this reason I have sent you Timothy, who is my beloved and faithful child in [the] Lord, who will remind you of my ways in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus, just as I teach everywhere in every church.

R.17: That is why I have sent Timothy to you. He is like a son to me, and I love him. He is faithful to the Lord. He will help you remember how I live as one who belongs to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus. That is what I teach in every church, wherever I go.

decisions.choice: I have sent: Timothy has already set out
alternatives: I am sending, with this letter (Timothy as its carrier)
decisions.reason: ἔπεμψα could be a letter-writer's past tense, written from the reader's point of view. But 16:10 says "if Timothy comes", so he was not carrying the letter; Acts 19:22 says Paul sent him ahead through Macedonia. He was on his way and would arrive after the letter.

decisions.choice: Paul's own child in the faith, trustworthy in the Lord's service
decisions.reason: Paul calls Timothy his τέκνον because Timothy came to faith or grew in it through him (1 Timothy 1:2; Philippians 2:22). πιστὸν means reliable: he can be trusted to represent Paul. It continues the father picture of verses 14-15.

decisions.choice: my ways: the way of life Paul lives and teaches as one who belongs to Christ
decisions.reason: "Way" for a manner of life is common in the Scriptures (Psalm 1:6). Paul's "ways in Christ Jesus" are the conduct and the teaching that go together, as the next clause, "as I teach everywhere", shows.

decisions.choice: like a son to me
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "child", which carries the family picture of verses 14-15 without adding a gender to the word. Readable says "son" because a grown man called someone's "child" sounds odd to a young reader; Timothy was a man.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

records.source: ὡς μὴ ἐρχομένου δέ μου πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐφυσιώθησάν τινες·
records.gloss: As not coming but of me to you, were puffed up some;
pieces: Some have become puffed up, assuming that I will never come to see you.

L.18: But as though I were not coming to you, some have become puffed up.

R.18: Some of you have become proud. They think I will not come to see you again.

decisions.choice: as if I were not coming: what some supposed
decisions.reason: ὡς with the genitive phrase gives the reason as those people saw it, not as a fact. Paul answers it at once in verse 19.

decisions.choice: some have become arrogant
decisions.reason: ἐφυσιώθησάν is the verb of 4:6. τινες points to a group within the church, not the whole congregation, perhaps those who set themselves up against Paul.

decisions.choice: puffed up
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the same picture as in verse 6 and verse 19, so the reader can see the repeated word; Readable says "proud".

records.source: ἐλεύσομαι δὲ ταχέως πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ἐὰν ὁ κύριος θελήσῃ, καὶ γνώσομαι οὐ τὸν λόγον τῶν πεφυσιωμένων ἀλλὰ τὴν δύναμιν, οὐ γὰρ ἐν λόγῳ ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἀλλ’ ἐν δυνάμει.
records.gloss: I will come but soon to you, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the word of those having been puffed up but the power; \v 20 not for in word the kingdom of the God but in power.
pieces: But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills. Then I will learn, not what these puffed-up people say, but whether they have any power.
For the kingdom of God shows itself in power, not in words.

L.19: But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the word of those who are puffed up but [their] power.
L.20: For the kingdom of God [is] not in word but in power.

R.19: But if the Lord wants me to, I will come to you soon. Then I will not care about what these proud people say. I will find out whether they have real power.
R.20: When God rules, it is not words that count but power.

decisions.choice: if the Lord wills: a reverent condition on future plans
decisions.reason: Paul makes his travel plans depend on the Lord's will, as in 16:7 and as James 4:15 teaches. He fully intends to come.

decisions.choice: word and power: impressive talk set against the real working of God's power
decisions.reason: Paul has contrasted clever speech with "the demonstration of the Spirit and of power" (2:4-5; compare 1:17-18). The power he will look for is what God's Spirit does in and through people, not their skill in speaking or their influence.

decisions.choice: the kingdom of God: God's rule, already at work now and still to come in full
decisions.reason: Here βασιλεία is God's reign shown in present power, as in Romans 14:17. Elsewhere in this letter it is the inheritance still to come (6:9-10; 15:50); both belong to Paul's teaching.

decisions.choice: the kingdom of God shows itself in power, not in words
alternatives: the kingdom of God is in power
decisions.reason: The Greek clause has no verb. Balanced supplies one that keeps the contrast: God's kingdom is seen where his power works.

decisions.choice: When God rules
decisions.reason: For a young reader "kingdom" suggests a country. Readable says what the phrase means here (m3).

records.source: τί θέλετε;
records.gloss: What do you want?
pieces: Which do you prefer?

decisions.choice: what do you want: introducing a choice between two ways Paul could come
alternatives: one question with the next sentence
decisions.reason: The question is answered by the two options that follow; the choice is the Corinthians' to make by how they respond to the letter.

decisions.choice: Which do you prefer? (B); Which would you like? (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that a choice between two things is coming.

records.source: ἐν ῥάβδῳ ἔλθω πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ἢ ἐν ἀγάπῃ πνεύματί τε πραΰτητος;
records.gloss: With rod should I come to you, or in love and spirit of gentleness?
pieces: Am I to come to you with a rod, or with love and gentleness of spirit?

L.21: Should I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?

R.21: Should I come to punish you, like a father with a stick? Or should I come with love and be gentle with you?

decisions.choice: a rod: the stick a father or guardian used to discipline a child
decisions.reason: ῥάβδῳ continues the picture of the father and the guardian (verse 15), who disciplined children with a rod (Proverbs 13:24). Paul means coming with authority to correct them (compare 2 Corinthians 13:2, 10).

decisions.choice: a spirit of gentleness: a gentle disposition
alternatives: the Holy Spirit, who gives gentleness
decisions.reason: πνεύματί here describes Paul's attitude, as in Galatians 6:1. Gentleness is the Spirit's fruit (Galatians 5:23), so a reference to the Holy Spirit is possible, but the contrast with the rod points to the manner in which Paul comes.

decisions.choice: with a rod ... in love: the same preposition for both ways of coming
decisions.reason: ἐν marks what Paul would come equipped with; with love it describes the manner. Love does not exclude discipline; the question is which the church will make necessary.

decisions.choice: to punish you, like a father with a stick
decisions.reason: Readable explains what the rod stands for (m1).
